description: We are a student organization from Ted Rönesans Koleji which make games.
summary:
Our project, **“Green Astronauts for a Green Mars,”** is an educational simulation game designed to teach students how biology and engineering are connected in space exploration. The game focuses on maintaining a greenhouse on Mars during unexpected power outages and resource shortages. Players face different crisis scenarios and must make decisions about how to use limited energy and resources while keeping the greenhouse stable.

The project teaches important concepts such as photosynthesis, light-dependent reactions, the Calvin cycle, ATP, and NADPH. At the same time, it develops critical thinking, problem-solving, risk assessment, and resource-management skills. Our target users are aspiring astronauts, students, and mission trainers, especially learners aged 7–12.

This project is important because astronauts may face limited resources and unexpected failures during future missions. By turning these challenges into an interactive game, we make complex biological and space-related concepts easier and more engaging to understand.
details:
Our project, “Green Astronauts for a Green Mars,” is a simulation-based educational game that challenges players to manage a greenhouse on Mars during unexpected power outages and resource shortages. Players encounter different crisis scenarios and must choose the best possible solution while working with limited energy and resources. The game uses clickable boxes and event cards to create a simple and interactive experience.

The main benefit of our project is that it combines biology with engineering and teaches students how important biology can be during space missions. It develops critical thinking, problem-solving, risk assessment, and resource-management skills while introducing concepts such as photosynthesis, light-dependent reactions, the Calvin cycle, ATP, and NADPH.

Our intended impact is to help students, future astronauts, and mission trainers understand how biological life-support systems can depend on energy and resource management. We designed the project especially for learners aged 7–12 and aimed to make complex scientific ideas easier and more engaging to learn.

For development, our project used a simple graphical user interface with clickable boxes and gameplay event cards. The presentation does not specify a particular programming language or hardware. We tested the gameplay mechanics, identified errors, and refined the event cards to balance difficulty and scientific accuracy.

The creative aspect of our project comes from turning a real space-exploration challenge into an educational game. Our team considered scientific accuracy, educational value, age-appropriateness, difficulty, resource limitations, and how to make decision-making engaging for players.
